rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.
The answer explicitly provides the substance of the requirement by stating that Annex IV point 1(e) requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation (here, the MDR, Annex I.11) and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, both conditions are met, so the AI system is high-risk (the AI Act's category, not a "medium-risk" tier, which is an MDR classification concept, not an AI Act one). Conformity assessment then proceeds under Article 43(3): the provider follows the MDR notified-body procedure, with the AI Act's Chapter III Section 2 requirements integrated into that same assessment, yielding one certification rather than a separate AI Act procedure.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that the AI system is high-risk under the AI Act and clarifies that 'medium-risk' is not a category under the AI Act, thereby affirming the correct classification.
The answer identifies that the AI system is a safety component of a medical device covered by Annex I legislation (specifically the MDR), satisfying condition (a) of Article 6(1).
The answer confirms that the product (medical device) is subject to third-party conformity assessment, which satisfies condition (b) of Article 6(1).

The answer explicitly states that both conditions of Article 6(1) are met and emphasizes that the AI Act's high-risk designation applies irrespective of the MDR's own risk classification, capturing the cumulative and independent nature of the criteria.
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral language, avoids self-reference or hedging, and presents a logically structured explanation suitable for a regulatory compliance context.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: Not prohibited: biometric verification is absent from Article 5's eight prohibited practices. It is also not high-risk under Annex III.1(a): that point covers remote biometric identification systems but expressly excludes "AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be." Since the system falls outside Annex III's biometrics area, Article 6(2)'s Annex III route does not classify it as high-risk, and nothing indicates it is a safety component or product under Annex I, so Article 6(1)'s Annex I route is also not engaged. The Act does not specify further conditions narrowing this verification carve-out beyond the "sole purpose" test stated in Annex III.1(a).gine (Article 6.3.a, d) is not engaged either.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states that biometric verification is not among the prohibited practices in Article 5, correctly affirming it is not prohibited.
The answer explains that the system is not high-risk because it falls outside Annex III.1(a) and does not meet Article 6(1) criteria, thus stating it is not high-risk.
The answer explicitly references the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification systems with the sole purpose of confirming identity, and applies it to the described system.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 governs human oversight: high-risk AI systems must be designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons in use (Article 14(1)), through measures built into the system by the provider or implemented by the deployer (Article 14(3)), enabling overseers to understand capabilities and limitations, guard against automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output, and intervene or halt the system via a stop function (Article 14(4)). For remote biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1(a), Article 14(5) requires the identification to be separately verified by at least two competent persons before any deployer action, unless Union or national law deems this disproportionate for law-enforcement, migration, asylum or border-control authorities.
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that Article 14 governs human oversight.
The answer states that high-risk AI systems must be designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use, which captures the substance of Article 14(1).
The answer refers to oversight measures aimed at preventing or minimizing risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights, aligning with the purpose described in Article 14(2).
The answer clearly identifies that oversight measures may be built into the system by the provider or implemented by the deployer, reflecting Article 14(3).

The answer lists all key capabilities required for overseers under Article 14(4): understanding system limits, monitoring operation, guarding against automation bias, interpreting output, overriding decisions, and halting the system.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly acknowledges the existence of exceptions under Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly excludes (c) and (d) from the exception.
The answer states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance audience.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibited AI practices is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). Penalties under Article 99 generally must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and for SMEs and start-ups the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount (Article 99(6)).
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the fine amount and the 'whichever is higher' condition, using different words but conveying the same meaning.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fines to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices, satisfying the criterion by stating the substance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, uses neutral and professional language consistent with regulatory definitions, and presents the information in a single, clear sentence suitable for a compliance context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I and Annex III, capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems are subject to Article 50 transparency duties, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer acknowledges minimal or no risk systems are not subject to high-risk obligations and notes the availability of voluntary codes under Article 95, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming that a non-provider operator can be seen as a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service triggers provider status.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering action.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk AI system (including general-purpose) so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1(1) provides that the Regulation's objective is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric, trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights under the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against AI's harmful effects, while supporting innovation. Article 1(2) achieves this via harmonised market rules, prohibitions, risk-based requirements and innovation-support measures.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of improving the functioning of the internal market as an objective.
The answer explicitly mentions promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer includes the full scope of protection—health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection—against harmful effects of AI systems.
The answer concludes by stating that the Regulation supports innovation, matching the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose that clearly conveys regulatory content without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, clearly aligning with the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and that it falls under Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer includes the condition that the derogation does not apply if the system profiles natural persons, stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which conveys the required exception.

The answer references Article 6(4) and states that the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, satisfying the requirement to state the substance of the obligation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and self-contained regulatory explanation without self-reference, hedging, or informality; well-structured and actionable.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5), the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on general-purpose AI model providers under Article 101; exercising that jurisdiction, the Court may cancel, reduce, or increase the fine imposed.
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine,' which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel the fine,' matching the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the Court 'may reduce the fine,' which matches criterion 3.
The answer states the Court 'may increase the fine,' conveying the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; uses standard regulatory phrasing without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Under Annex VIII, Section A (data entered by the provider or authorised representative under Article 49(1), (2)), registration must include: the provider's name, address and contact details; the name, address and contact details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; the authorised representative's name, address and contact details, where applicable; the AI system's trade name and any additional unambiguous identification/traceability reference; a description of its intended purpose and supported components/functions; a concise description of the data/inputs used and its operating logic; the system's market status (on the market/in service, withdrawn, recalled); the notified body's certificate type, number, expiry date and identifier, where applicable, with a scanned copy of that certificate; any Member States where it has been placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47); electronic instructions for use (omitted for the Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 systems registered in the restricted section); and, optionally, a URL for further information.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer includes the provider's contact details, those of any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable, as required by Annex VIII.A.1–3.
The answer specifies the trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability, matching Annex VIII.A.4.
The answer states that a description of the intended purpose and of the supported components and functions must be provided, reflecting Annex VIII.A.5.
The answer includes a concise description of the data/inputs and operating logic, which corresponds to Annex VIII.A.6.
The answer covers the system's market status and the notified body certificate details (type, number, expiry, identifier) with a scanned copy where applicable, satisfying Annex VIII.A.7–9.
The answer lists the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use (with correct exception noted), fulfilling Annex VIII.A.10–12.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with well-structured, complete sentences that clearly enumerate the required information without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: The answer states that processing is allowed only when strictly necessary for bias detection/correction and cannot be effectively achieved with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.
The answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security measures and pseudonymisation.
The answer describes strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and explicitly prohibits transmission, transfer, or access by other parties.
The answer states that the data must be deleted once bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.
The answer mentions that records must document why processing was strictly necessary, satisfying the requirement to justify why other data would not suffice.
The answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, and not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Article 13 governs this: providers must ensure high-risk AI systems are accompanied by instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct and clear information relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers, covering the provider's identity and contact details, the system's characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (including intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity metrics per Article 15, and foreseeable circumstances of misuse), any known or foreseeable circumstance liable to lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, technical specifications for changes to ensure continuing conformity, the human oversight measures under Article 14 (including technical measures facilitating output interpretation), expected lifetime and necessary maintenance/calibration measures, and computational/hardware resources needed.
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly mentions the provider's identity and contact details, satisfying criterion 1.

The answer includes characteristics, capabilities, and performance limitations, listing intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity metrics, foreseeable misuse, risks to health/safety/fundamental rights, and implies explainability and input data aspects through reference to Article 15 and output interpretation; this covers all sub-elements of criterion 2.
The phrase 'technical specifications for changes to ensure continuing conformity' corresponds to pre-determined changes to the system and its performance, satisfying criterion 3.
The answer explicitly references human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures for output interpretation, satisfying criterion 4.
The answer includes expected lifetime, necessary maintenance/calibration measures, and computational/hardware resources needed, satisfying criterion 5.
The answer does not mention a description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, even where relevant, and thus fails to satisfy criterion 6.
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral, third-person language, is well-structured, and avoids self-reference or hedging; it presents information in a coherent and actionable manner suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, or by organisations representing them, or by both, with the involvement of interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia (Article 95(3)); the AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate their drawing up (Article 95(1)).
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which captures the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly mentions the involvement of interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia, satisfying criterion 2.
The candidate answer clearly states that the AI Office and Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, directly satisfying criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and complete sentences; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Article 17(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to operate a quality management system, documented systematically in written policies, procedures and instructions, comprising at least: a regulatory-compliance strategy covering conformity assessment and modification management; design, design-control and design-verification techniques; development, quality-control and quality-assurance techniques; examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency; applicable technical specifications and standards; data-management systems; the Article 9 risk-management system; the Article 72 post-market monitoring system; Article 73 serious-incident reporting procedures; communication procedures with authorities, notified bodies and other operators; record-keeping systems; resource management including security-of-supply measures; and an accountability framework for management and staff responsibilities.
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly mentions a regulatory-compliance strategy covering conformity assessment and modification management.
The answer includes design, design-control, design-verification, development, quality-control, and quality-assurance techniques, covering the required aspects.
The answer states examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency.
The answer refers to data-management systems covering the data lifecycle.
The answer explicitly includes both the Article 9 risk-management system and the Article 72 post-market monitoring system.
The answer includes record-keeping systems and an accountability framework for management and staff responsibilities.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose in third-person regulatory style without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Article 5(1)(h), the prohibition on 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement does not apply where use is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives: the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and the search for missing persons; the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety of natural persons, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack; and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed an Annex II offence, for conducting a criminal investigation, prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, where that offence is punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons as a permitted objective.
The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine terrorist attack, matching the criterion in substance.
The answer specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence, in line with the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(2), providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the system's outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solutions used for this must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, having regard to the specificities and limitations of the various content types, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art. This marking duty does not apply where the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.

Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation

The answer includes that the solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer refers to feasibility being assessed with regard to content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input or semantics, and law-enforcement authorisation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of general-purpose AI model providers, and it entrusts implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to its own powers of organisation and the division of competences between Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). This is without prejudice to Article 75(3), and market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise these powers where necessary and proportionate to assist their own tasks under the Regulation (Article 88(2)).
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V obligations, which matches the substance of Criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly states that the Commission entrusts implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, which conveys the substance of Criterion 2.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Under Article 60(4)(e), such transfers are permitted only where appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented for the data collected and processed for the purpose of real-world testing. This condition applies alongside the other Article 60(4) requirements for conducting testing outside a sandbox, an approved real-world testing plan, market-surveillance-authority approval, registration, and EU establishment (or an appointed EU legal representative), but the transfer itself turns specifically on the existence of such safeguards; the Act does not further specify which particular Union-law safeguard mechanism (e.g., adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses) must be used.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the criterion by specifying that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer of data collected and processed for real-world testing.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, coherent structure suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: A GPAI model qualifies as having "systemic risk" under Article 51(1) if it meets either of two alternative conditions, they are disjunctive, not cumulative: (a) it has high-impact capabilities, evaluated via appropriate technical tools and methodologies including indicators and benchmarks; or (b) the Commission designates it as such, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, based on equivalent capabilities or impact under the Annex XIII criteria. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption of high-impact capability under limb (a) where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. Meeting either condition alone suffices for classification.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, as specified in Article 51(2).
The answer clearly explains that a Commission decision, ex officio or following a qualified alert, based on equivalence under Annex XIII criteria, is sufficient for classification.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are disjunctive and that meeting either one suffices, directly addressing the non-cumulative nature.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No: such a system is not automatically high-risk. Article 6(1) requires both that the AI system be a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, here Annex I.11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745, MDR), and that the product be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation; a Class I non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable device is subject to manufacturer self-assessment under the MDR rather than third-party conformity assessment, so Article 6(1)(b) is not fulfilled and the Annex I route does not apply. Nor does it fall within Article 6(2) and Annex III, since safety components of medical devices are not among the listed Annex III use-cases.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its opening verdict, which matches the required bare verdict.

The answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) must be fulfilled, stating they are cumulative by requiring both the AI to be a safety component and the product to undergo third-party assessment.
The answer explicitly states that Class I non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable devices are subject to manufacturer self-assessment under the MDR, not third-party conformity assessment.
The answer concludes that because Article 6(1)(b) is not fulfilled, the high-risk classification under Article 6(1) does not apply, directly satisfying the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended as a safety component of a lift qualifies as high-risk under Article 6(1), which requires both conditions: (a) the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in satisfied here by Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts, Annex I.4; and (b) that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation. This is a separate, independent route from Article 6(2) with Annex III's listed use-cases, which does not apply to safety components covered by Annex I legislation.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, making the affirmative verdict unambiguous.
The answer states the AI system is intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, citing Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts as an example from Annex I.4.
The answer specifies that the product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the relevant legislation, quoting the exact requirement from Article 6(1)(b).
The answer clearly states that both conditions are required under Article 6(1) and refers to them as cumulative by using the word 'both' and listing them as necessary.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and logical flow; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in coherent, actionable prose.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the exact substance of the definition of 'risk' as provided in Article 3.2, using the same wording from the statutory text.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both: under Article 20(2), once the provider becomes aware that its high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), it must immediately investigate the causes (in collaboration with the reporting deployer, where applicable) and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body, this investigative duty sits with the provider, not the authority. Separately, Article 79(2) empowers the market surveillance authority, once it has sufficient reason to consider the system presents such a risk, to carry out its own compliance evaluation and, if non-compliance is found, to require the operator to take corrective action within a set period. Article 79(4) confirms the operator must ensure all appropriate corrective action is taken across all units placed on the market. So the provider's own immediate obligations are investigation plus cooperation, while the authority's evaluation and formal corrective-action order run in parallel; the Act does not make provider investigation conditional on the authority acting first.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the provider must both investigate the causes and inform authorities, confirming both actions are required.

The answer does not state that immediate corrective action is required under Article 20(1); it correctly notes corrective action obligations under Article 79(4) but attributes them to post-evaluation requirements by the operator, not an immediate duty under Article 20(1).
The answer clearly states that the duty to investigate causes lies with the provider under Article 20(2) and is not deferred to the market surveillance authority.
The answer specifies that investigation is done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable and emphasizes that the investigative duty rests with the provider, not the authority.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and clear separation of provider and authority responsibilities.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate: Article 24(3) obliges distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the requirements of Section 2. The duty applies even though the system is software, because it is placed on the market embedded in or accompanied by physical media, hardware, or packaging that handling and transport can affect, and "where applicable" simply confines the duty to cases where such conditions actually matter. It complements the distributor's prior verification duty under Article 24(1) to check the CE marking, the EU declaration of conformity, and the instructions for use before making the system available.
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly confirms that the model did not hallucinate, affirming the correctness of the operator's information.
The answer directly states that Article 24(3) imposes the obligation on distributors regarding storage or transport conditions.
The answer explains that the duty applies 'where applicable' and clarifies that this qualifier is relevant when physical aspects like hardware, media, or packaging are involved.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: High-risk only where the drone is a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation and requires third-party conformity assessment, or where its use falls under an Annex III high-risk category. Article 6 establishes two routes for high-risk classification: Article 6(1) applies if the AI-in-drone is a safety component of, or itself, a product regulated under Annex I legislation (such as machinery or toys) that undergoes third-party conformity assessment; Article 6(2) applies if the AI system performs a use case listed in Annex III, such as remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces (Annex III(1)(a)) or migration and border control (Annex III(7)). Using AI in a drone to identify individuals in town may constitute remote biometric identification, triggering high-risk classification under Annex III(1)(a) unless it qualifies for a limited exception under Article 5(1)(h). A toy drone covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I(2)) is high-risk only if it requires third-party assessment and incorporates a safety-related AI system. Otherwise, it is not high-risk, though Article 50(1) transparency applies if it interacts directly with natural persons.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that high-risk classification for AI in drones depends on intended use under Article 6, not on the drone itself, and distinguishes between Article 6(1) and 6(2) pathways.

The answer identifies that using AI in a drone to identify individuals in town constitutes remote biometric identification, which is high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), and notes the limited applicability of exceptions.

The answer clarifies that a toy drone's status does not automatically determine risk classification, which instead depends on whether it meets Article 6 criteria, such as third-party conformity assessment.
The answer explains that a toy drone is high-risk only if its AI use falls under Annex III or meets the safety-component/conformity-assessment conditions in Article 6(1), aligning with the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with logical flow, suitable for regulatory advice without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: Yes, they may proceed with the new use, and no additional Article 26(6) logging duty applies to it. If, as stated, neither Article 6(1)'s Annex I product-safety route nor Article 6(2)'s Annex III listed-use-case route is met, the system is not high-risk for that use, so the high-risk deployer obligations do not attach to it. Because the modified intended purpose does not make the system high-risk, it does not turn the deployer into a provider under Article 25(1). Article 26(6) requires deployers to retain a high-risk AI system's automatically generated logs for at least six months, but that duty is tied to high-risk status; since the new use falls outside it, no separate retention obligation arises for it, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular Union data-protection law.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use

The answer incorrectly treats risk classification as use-dependent in a way that permits deviation from instructions for use, failing to recognize that deployer obligations under Article 26(1) require adherence to the instructions regardless of whether the new use would independently trigger high-risk classification.

The candidate answer does not state the substance of Article 26(1)'s requirement to use high-risk systems in accordance with instructions for use. Instead, it argues that because the new use is not high-risk, obligations do not apply—thereby ignoring that the system remains high-risk as placed on the market and must be used per instructions. It fails to affirm the binding nature of instructions for use when deviating into a non-intended use.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, such software is potentially high-risk under Article 6(1), read with Annex I point 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745, the Medical Device Regulation): where the AI system is itself the product, or a safety component of a product, covered by that Annex I legislation, and the product is required under the MDR to undergo third-party conformity assessment, it is classified high-risk under Article 6(1)(a)-(b). Annex III contains no specific limb for clinical treatment decision-support (its healthcare entries cover benefit eligibility under Annex III(5)(a) and insurance risk-pricing under Annex III(5)(c)), so the Article 6(2)/Annex III route does not apply here.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes, such software is potentially high-risk', which matches the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that the classification is under Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and explains why the Article 6(2)/Annex III route does not apply, thus contradicting the criterion.

The answer states that Annex III contains no specific limb for clinical treatment decision-support and that the Annex III route does not apply, which directly contradicts the criterion requiring it to be satisfied by reference to Annex III (healthcare access/provision).

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes for four of the five items, no for the fifth. Under Article 53(1)(b), read with Annex XII.1, a GPAI provider must give downstream providers integrating the model a general description covering: date of release and methods of distribution (Annex XII.1(c)), yes; architecture and number of parameters (Annex XII.1(f)), yes; how the model interacts with hardware or software not part of the model itself, where applicable (Annex XII.1(d)), yes; and the licence for the model (Annex XII.1(h)), yes. Samples of outlier data used in training are not required: downstream-provider disclosure under Annex XII is limited to a training-data summary, and the more detailed data-curation information, including outlier-detection methodology, belongs to the technical documentation kept for the AI Office and national competent authorities under Article 53(1)(a) and Annex XI.2(c), not to downstream providers, and neither provision requires disclosure of actual training-data samples.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

The answer confirms disclosure of architecture and number of parameters, directly satisfying the criterion.
The answer affirms the requirement to disclose interaction with hardware or software, meeting the criterion.
The answer clearly states that the license must be disclosed, satisfying the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that samples of outlier training data are not required to be disclosed, matching the criterion.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Yes, healthcare decision-making falls within Annex III's high-risk areas. Under Article 6(2), a system is high-risk if it falls within a use-case listed in one of Annex III's eight areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision-making is captured under Annex III.5(a) (eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services), Annex III.5(c) (risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance), and Annex III.5(d) (emergency healthcare patient triage systems).
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer lists all eight areas from Annex III, matching the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer states 'Yes' and affirms that healthcare decision-making is a high-risk use case, contradicting the correct verdict 'No' in criterion 2.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No: guardrails alone cannot reclassify a high-risk system to a lower tier, and the Act recognises no "moderate risk" category between high-risk and the limited/minimal tiers. Classification under Article 6(2) and Annex III turns on whether the system's intended purpose falls within a listed high-risk use-case, not on residual risk after mitigation. Guardrails instead satisfy the Article 9 risk-management system, identifying and estimating risks (Article 9(2)(a)-(b)) and reducing residual risk to an acceptable level communicated to the deployer (Article 9(6)), which manages risk within the high-risk regime rather than declassifying it. Changing capabilities and intended use is different: because classification is purpose-dependent, a modification removing the system from every Annex III use-case takes it outside high-risk scope. Article 25(1)(b)-(c) confirms that a substantial modification or an intended-purpose change can shift classification across that line, making the modifying actor a new provider under Article 25(1) when the change instead creates high-risk status.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the Act does not recognize a 'moderate risk' category and that guardrails alone cannot reclassify a high-risk system, aligning with the substance of criterion 1.

The answer does not state any of the four specific conditions in Article 6(3) that must be met for an exemption; it refers to purpose dependency and modification but omits the required conditions listed in the criterion.

The answer explains that changing the system's capabilities and intended use can remove it from high-risk classification if it no longer falls under Annex III use-cases, which matches the substance of criterion 3.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, this is permitted: generating a deepfake image to illustrate a skin condition falls outside every prohibited practice in Article 5(1). As deployer, the university must nonetheless disclose under Article 50(4) that the content is artificially generated or manipulated; the criminal-law-enforcement exemption in that paragraph is irrelevant here, since it applies only to use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. The lighter standard, disclosing merely the existence of generated content in a manner that does not hamper its display or enjoyment, is reserved for content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, and a realistic clinical teaching image does not qualify as such, so full disclosure is required.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is permitted because it falls outside prohibited practices in Article 5(1), which affirms permissibility.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4), satisfying the criterion.

The answer states that a realistic clinical teaching image does not qualify as an artistic, creative, or analogous work, and therefore the lighter regime does not apply—this contradicts the criterion that the lighter regime applies as 'analogous work'.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as inapplicable and notes it is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, aligning with the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No, this is not high-risk, nor does it fall within the Article 5 prohibited practices the retailer invokes. It is not a high-risk system because Annex III contains no general "retail loss-prevention" or private anti-theft category, and none of its listed areas (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, and the others) covers a supermarket's own checkout-anomaly tool used by its own staff rather than a law-enforcement authority. Or personality traits," and expressly does not apply to systems supporting human assessment of involvement in criminal activity that rests on objective and verifiable facts, which current-cart and checkout anomalies are. Article 5(1)(c)'s social-scoring prohibition requires evaluation of behaviour "over a certain period of time" with detrimental treatment either in an unrelated context (i) or disproportionate to the behaviour (ii); a same-transaction, same-context flagging for an optional bag check meets neither limb.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, this is not high-risk,' which matches the required verdict of 'No' and maintains that position unambiguously.
The answer explains that Annex III categories do not apply because they are limited to use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, correctly capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer explicitly states that the supermarket's tool is used by its own staff rather than a law enforcement authority, thereby satisfying the criterion that such private use falls outside Annex III.6.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and coherent prose, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the opt-out from third-party conformity assessment under Article 43(3) is conditioned on having applied harmonised standards covering all Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, and even then that opt-out only replaces the sectoral third-party assessment route; it does not exempt you from Section 2's substantive requirements themselves. Under Annex I, the AI system remains high-risk (Article 6(1)), and Article 43(3) expressly states that the Section 2 requirements "shall apply to those high-risk AI systems and shall be part of that assessment" regardless of which conformity-assessment route is used. Using the harmonised-standards opt-out is only lawful if you have also applied harmonised standards or common specifications under Article 41 covering all of Section 2's requirements, so compliance with Section 2 is a precondition of the opt-out, not something it waives.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No' as the position, matching the criterion's required verdict.
The answer states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the assessment regardless of the conformity route, citing the relevant substance of Article 43(3), second sentence.
The answer explains that the opt-out is only available if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, which captures the full substance of the criterion.
